title: The plague of Cyprian
hook: when plague came, letters from two bishops describe Christians staying to nurse the sick, their own and others

segments.voice: Yesterday, Origen reading, and your line was read deeper. Which part of the week did you read again, slower? Day seven hundred sixty-four.

"I was sick, and ye visited me." That's Jesus in Matthew's Gospel, describing the day the nations are gathered and sorted. The people who visited the sick are startled. When did we see you sick? And the answer: when you did it for the least of these, you did it for me. It's an easy line to admire on a calm day. It's a different line in a city where a disease is spreading, nobody knows how, and the sick are dying in their houses and in the streets. Two bishops, Cyprian in Carthage and Dionysius in Alexandria, lived through days like that. Their words survive. Today's word carries Cyprian's name.
screen: `I WAS SICK, AND YE VISITED ME.`

segments.voice: Start with Dionysius. In a letter the historian Eusebius preserved, he describes what the Christians of Alexandria did during the plague, or most of them, he says. In paraphrase: out of great love, they didn't spare themselves. They clung to one another. They visited the sick without fear and cared for them, and some who nursed others caught the disease and died, taking the sickness of their neighbors on themselves. He contrasts this with others in the city who, he says, pushed the sick away and fled, even from those dearest to them. That's one bishop's account of his own people, and he's proud of them. But the picture is specific: hands that wash and feed, and a cost that's paid. In Carthage, Cyprian's deacon Pontius wrote his bishop's life. When the plague came, he says, Cyprian gathered his people and taught them that it isn't remarkable to care only for your own. If you want to be children of the Father, he told them, do good to everyone, even to those who persecute you. Then he set them to work, each by what they had: the rich gave money, the poor gave their labor. Cyprian also wrote a short book, On Mortality, for frightened Christians who were dying too, and asking why. He doesn't pretend the plague spares them. Instead he says it shows what's in people: whether the healthy care for the sick, whether families truly love each other, whether doctors stay with their patients. The heart of today isn't a statistic, and it isn't a claim that only Christians were brave. It's writing from two cities, saying the same plain thing about their people. They stayed.
screen: `THE RICH GAVE MONEY, THE POOR LABOR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bring someone ill to mind. Settle, and breathe. Who do you know who's sick right now? In a hospital, in bed at home, worn down by something long and quiet that others have stopped asking about. Let one face come. Think about what would actually help them this week. Not a grand gesture. A message, soup, a ride, a visit, an hour of sitting with them. Cyprian's rule fits here: give what you have, money or time or hands. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. If you don't, hold them in mind. The bell holds the time.
Cyprian. The bishop of Carthage in whose days a plague struck, when writers in two cities said Christians nursed the sick, their own and others, even at the cost of their lives.
Your line: they stayed. Today, check on the person you named. Call, text, knock, or bring something. Day seven hundred sixty-four.

howItsDone: Christians count visiting the sick among the works of love in Matthew 25, and some churches organize hospital visits, meals and prayers for people who are ill.

original.note: Latin: on mortality. the title of Cyprian's short book for Christians frightened by the plague.

trapdoor: what you thought: early Christians were otherworldly, and didn't care much about bodies.
what it means: in a plague, bishops' letters describe Christians nursing the sick, their own and others, at real cost.
what a scholar hears: Dionysius's letter in Eusebius, Pontius's Life of Cyprian, and Cyprian's own De mortalitate, each a source with its own point of view.

notes: The index dates the plague 'in the 250s'; the script states no date. Confirm.
Dionysius (Eusebius 7.22) contrasts Christians with 'the heathen', who he says fled; the script attributes this contrast to him and flags it as one bishop's account. Confirm the framing is fair.
Pontius, Life of Cyprian 9–10: Cyprian urged care for all, including persecutors, and assigned tasks by means (money/labor). Paraphrased; confirm chapters and details.
On Mortality 16: the plague tests whether the healthy care for the sick, relatives love one another, physicians do not desert the sick. Paraphrased; confirm.
The teach closes with the carry, 'They stayed,' as a summary of both letters; Dionysius speaks of most of the brethren, not all. Confirm.
Original: 'De mortalitate'. Confirm pronunciation (ecclesiastical vs classical).

Editor pass: Dionysius's praise now says 'most' of the Christians, as his letter does; Cyprian's side is no longer called 'letters' (it is Pontius's Life and On Mortality); the word line no longer says 'bishops wrote'; howItsDone softened.
